method: A rotary or electronic shutter is open for the shutter angle divided by 360 of each frame interval, so the exposure is angle / (360 x fps): 180 degrees at 24 fps is 1/48 s and 172.8 degrees at 24 fps is exactly 1/50 s. During that exposure a subject moving across the frame at a constant speed travels speed x exposure, and the pinhole projection onto the sensor scales that travel by the focal length divided by the subject distance, giving the smear on the sensor in millimetres. The sensor width divided by the capture width gives pixels per millimetre, and the sensor smear times that scale is the blur in pixels; the same value over the capture width is the blur as a share of the frame, which does not change with resolution. The page also reports the frame width at the subject distance (sensor width x distance / focal length), the horizontal field of view 2 x atan(sensor width / (2 x focal length)) and a table of the blur at 45, 90, 144, 172.8, 180, 270 and 360 degrees. A camera pan of one radian per second smears the image exactly like a subject moving at that many metres per second at that distance, because the image travel is the focal length times the angle swept. The model assumes a thin lens, a subject at one distance moving perpendicular to the optical axis at constant speed, and a uniform exposure with no rolling-shutter readout; depth of field, focus breathing, stabilisation, lens distortion and subjects at other distances are not modelled, and a real sensor's blur also depends on the aperture's own diffraction. Inputs allow 1 to 240 fps, 1 to 360 degrees, 1 to 2000 mm focal length, 1 to 100 mm sensor width, 64 to 16384 px capture width, 0.05 to 100000 m distance and 0 to 1000 m/s speed. Blank, non-numeric, fractional-pixel and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Rotary disc shutter - Wikipedia: the shutter angle over 360 equals the exposure time over the frame interval, and the angle is adjusted to control motion blur
Pinhole camera model - Wikipedia: image-plane coordinates are the focal length times the scene coordinates divided by depth, which is the magnification used here
